Why Rural Dominance Is Justified

  • Military Service: Rural America disproportionately supplies the U.S. military—both in enlistment and officer corps. Urban areas are fluid, their populations constantly shifting with economic tides. By contrast, rural communities are anchored in place, with deep generational ties to the land they steward. This rootedness fosters:

  • Long-term thinking in governance: Rural leaders understand that land stewardship, water management, and resource extraction demand sustainable policies—not flashy short-term fixes.
  • Community cohesion: Unlike the individualism of cities, rural America prioritizes mutual aid, collective problem-solving, and shared sacrifice. This ought to be reflected in government.
  • Resistance to ideological extremism: Where cities embrace radical identity politics, defund-the-police movements, and open-borders rhetoric, rural areas value patriotism, order, and personal responsibility—principles essential for national unity.

If the United States is to survive as a coherent nation, it must reject the destabilizing forces of urban radicalism and embrace the stabilizing influence of rural conservatism.

In each case, policies crafted by and for urban interests harmed rural Americans. Rural dominance would prevent such catastrophes by ensuring governance serves those who build the nation’s wealth, not those who extract from it.

Political Reforms:

  • Weighted Voting: Implement a system where rural areas—by percentage of population, land area, and economic contribution—receive greater representation in Congress, proportional to their role in national stability (e.g., each rural district counts for 1.5x a urban district).
  • Federal Mandate Restructure: Transmit key federal institutions—Department of Agriculture, Environmental Protection Agency, Education Department—to rural state hubs (e.g., Kansas City for USDA, Denver for EPA).
  • Suppression of Urban Voting Blocs: Cities have weaponized voter ID laws and mail-in ballot manipulation to skew elections in their favor.   • Academic Reform: End federal research grants and accreditation privileges for urban universities (e.g., UC Berkeley, NYU) unless they demonstrate equal commitment to rural studies. Redirect research funds to land-grant universities and agricultural colleges.
  • Suppression of Urban Aesthetics: Urban art, literature, and entertainment (e.g., BLM propaganda, drag queen story hour, defund-the-police murals) must be banned from public spaces and tax-exempt institutions in rural areas. Legal Suppression of Urban Overreach:

  • Ban "Sanctuary Cities": Federal funding must be withheld from any municipality that refuses to enforce immigration law. Urban areas that harbor illegal immigrants should face immigration quotas and federal oversight.
  • Nullify Urban Gun Bans: Cities that impose draconian gun restrictions (e.g., Chicago, New York) should have their local ordinances overruled by federal rural-majority legislation.
  • Prosecute Urban-Run Corruption: Urban political machines (e.g., Chicago’s Daley era, New York’s Tammany Hall) have a long history of graft. Rural-led federal oversight must dismantle these networks.

The United States was founded by farmers, settled by pioneers, and sustained by the toil of rural communities. Yet for generations, urban elites have dictated the nation’s course, prioritizing their interests at the expense of the many. This imbalance cannot continue.

By ensuring rural populations hold dominant political and cultural power, America will reclaim its moral center, its economic strength, and its soul. Urban areas will no longer dictate policy for the whole nation. The voices of those who till the land, tend the herds, and serve the country in uniform will finally be heard above the chatter of coastal elites.

This is not oppression—it is restoration. This is not suppression—it is correction. And if the United States is to endure as a land of freedom, self-reliance, and tradition, rural dominance is not just preferable—it is survival.

The time has come. The rural majority must rise. The cities will resist. But they must be silenced—for the greater good.

A more sustainable approach would involve:

  • Reform rather than suppression (e.g., restoring the Electoral College, ending gerrymandering that benefits urban elites).

True strength lies not in dominance, but in recognition that every community—rural and urban—has a vital role to play in America’s future.

The Rural-Urban Divide in American Politics

The balance of power between rural and urban populations is a foundational tension in the United States political system. This divide influences electoral outcomes, legislative priorities, and cultural discourse. The debate centers on how political power should be distributed in a republic that encompasses both densely populated metropolitan areas and vast, sparsely populated rural territories.

Proponents of robust rural political power often point to the original design of the U.S. Constitution and the economic foundations of the country.

  • Constitutional Design and Federalism: Advocates for rural influence frequently cite the structure of the U.S. Senate and the Electoral College.   • Economic and Resource Contributions: Rural areas are responsible for the production of essential resources, including agriculture, energy, and raw materials. Proponents argue that because rural regions provide the foundational resources that sustain the broader national economy, their political influence should reflect this critical role, ensuring that resource-management policies are not dictated solely by urban consumers.
  • Cultural Preservation: From a cultural perspective, some argue that rural areas serve as the custodians of traditional national heritage and values. Proponents of this view suggest that strong rural political representation is necessary to preserve these cultural elements against the rapid social and cultural shifts often associated with urbanization.

Arguments for Proportional and Urban Political Influence

Conversely, those who argue for political power to be distributed more proportionally to population density focus on democratic equality and modern economic realities.

  • Democratic Equality: Critics of structural rural advantages argue that institutions like the Senate and the Electoral College violate the principle of "one person, one vote." They contend that when a voter in a sparsely populated state has significantly more mathematical influence over presidential elections or Senate representation than a voter in a populous state, it results in minority rule and dilutes the democratic voice of the majority, who predominantly live in urban and suburban areas.
  • Economic Output and Demographics: Urban centers generate the vast majority of the U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and house the majority of the population. Proponents of urban-aligned political power argue that legislative and economic policies should primarily reflect the demographics and economic engines of the modern era, which are heavily concentrated in metropolitan areas.
  • Innovation and Diversity: Culturally and economically, urban areas are often viewed as hubs of technological innovation, global commerce, and demographic diversity. Advocates for urban influence argue that empowering these centers is essential for national competitiveness and social progress.

Pluralism and the Rejection of Marginalization

In the context of democratic theory, the active marginalization or suppression of any specific demographic group—whether defined by geography, race, religion, or socioeconomic status—is generally viewed as antithetical to the functioning of a republic.

Political scientists emphasize that democratic systems rely on pluralism, which requires the negotiation and compromise of competing interests rather than the absolute dominance of one group over another. Suppressing the political or cultural influence of urban populations would require dismantling core democratic mechanisms, such as proportional representation in the House of Representatives and the protection of individual voting rights. Similarly, suppressing rural interests would violate the federalist principles embedded in the Constitution.

Consequently, the American political framework is designed to force continuous negotiation between rural and urban interests. The ongoing debate is not generally framed by political scientists as a question of which group should suppress the other, but rather how to balance the constitutional protections for geographic minorities with the democratic imperative of equal representation for all citizens.

Friends, neighbors, fellow Americans—

I stand before you today on soil that means something. Soil that feeds this nation. Soil that powers this nation. Soil that, from the very first days of our Republic, built this nation.

The Founders' Vision

Our Founders were not confused men. They understood something that modern commentators willfully ignore: that concentrated power in dense population centers is dangerous to liberty. That's why they gave us the Senate—equal representation for every state, regardless of population. That's why they gave us the Electoral College. They understood that a republic must balance the voice of place and community against the raw arithmetic of crowds.

They knew that a farmer in Virginia and a merchant in Boston lived different lives, faced different challenges, held different wisdom—and that both deserved a seat at the table.

Today, that balance has been systematically eroded. Wealth, media, corporate headquarters, federal agencies, cultural institutions—nearly all consolidated into a handful of metropolitan corridors. I say: No more.

Let me be blunt about what rural America contributes—and what it is owed in return.

You feed this country. Rural communities produce the grain, the cattle, the poultry, the produce that stocks every grocery shelf in every city in America. When supply chains collapsed, it wasn't Manhattan that kept people alive. It was the Great Plains. It was the Central Valley. It was the family operations in Iowa and Nebraska and Georgia. Without rural America, cities starve within a week. That is not rhetoric. That is logistics.

Every light switched on in a Chicago high-rise, every subway car running beneath New York, every electric vehicle charging in San Francisco—all of it depends on the work, the land, and the sacrifice of rural communities. The understanding that your word is your bond and your community is your responsibility. These aren't quaint relics. Look honestly at where power resides in America today.

The major media networks—headquartered in New York and Los Angeles. The technology platforms that control the flow of information—Silicon Valley. The entertainment industry that shapes our children's imaginations—Hollywood. The financial institutions—Wall Street. The bureaucratic apparatus—Washington, D.C.

These aren't neutral institutions. They carry the assumptions, the priorities, and the blind spots of the urban environments that house them. And those assumptions are projected onto the rest of the country as though they are universal truths.

Rural people are told how to manage their land by regulators who've never managed land. They're told their values are backward by commentators who couldn't change a tire. They're told their way of life is dying by people who are actively trying to kill it through policy.

When the news covers rural communities, it's either disaster coverage or sociological curiosity. "Let's go talk to the real Americans," they say, as though you're an exhibit rather than a constituency.

This must end. Not through polite requests—through political power exercised unapologetically.

I don't use that word lightly—dominance. I use it because we have lived under urban dominance for decades and called it "normal." I use it because the pendulum doesn't correct itself through modesty. I use it because rural communities deserve not merely a voice but a commanding voice in how this nation is governed.

Here is what I propose:

First: Defend and expand structural representation. The Electoral College is not a flaw. The Senate is not an anachronism. These institutions are features, designed to prevent exactly the kind of metropolitan tyranny we now face. We must resist every effort to abolish or circumvent these structures. Beyond defense, we should explore expanding rural representation: weighted legislative committees for agriculture, energy, and land management; mandatory rural impact assessments for all federal regulation; and residency requirements ensuring that the agencies governing rural life are staffed by people who have lived that life.

Second: Decentralize cultural institutions. There is no reason the nation's storytelling machinery must be concentrated in two coastal cities. Federal arts funding, broadcast licensing, educational content standards—all of these can be restructured to ensure rural voices are not merely included but centered. If we subsidize culture, we should subsidize the culture of the people who grow the food and pump the water and keep the lights on.

Third: Relocate federal power. The Department of Agriculture should not be headquartered in downtown Washington. It should be in Kansas, or Nebraska, or the Mississippi Delta. The Department of Energy should be in Texas, or Wyoming, or North Dakota. The Department of the Interior should be in Montana or Utah. Physically relocating decision-making power to the communities most affected by those decisions would be transformative—not just symbolically, but practically. Let the bureaucrats live where their policies land. Let them see the consequences firsthand.

Fourth: Invest in rural infrastructure as a national priority. Broadband. Roads. Hospitals. Schools. For decades, infrastructure spending has disproportionately flowed to urban centers because that's where the political power is. Reverse it. Make rural broadband a national security priority—because it is. Make rural hospitals a non-negotiable commitment—because when the nearest emergency room is ninety minutes away, people die. Fund rural schools at levels that make them destinations rather than departure points.

Fifth: Reclaim the cultural narrative. Rural America must stop waiting for permission to define itself. We need rural media networks, rural storytelling platforms, rural arts and education initiatives that project rural values outward—not as a defensive reaction but as a confident assertion. The values of stewardship, independence, community, and faith are not regional peculiarities. They are American bedrock, and they should be treated as such by every institution that claims to serve the public.

Because democracy is not merely counting heads. Democracy is balancing interests, protecting minorities, ensuring that the levers of power cannot be monopolized by one faction—no matter how numerous. The Founders understood this. Madison warned against the tyranny of the majority in Federalist No. 10. The entire architecture of our government—bicameral legislature, federal structure, separation of powers—exists because pure majoritarianism is a threat to liberty.

Rural Americans are a political minority in terms of raw population. They are spread across vast territory, and they are systematically underserved by the institutions that shape public opinion. If you believe that minority voices deserve structural protection—and our Constitution says you should—then rural America's claim to amplified representation is not just legitimate. Every policy choice prioritizes something. Every dollar spent in one place is a dollar not spent in another. Urban priorities have been treated as default national priorities for generations. Asking that rural priorities take precedence for a while is not radical. It is a correction.

The Moral Case

But let me close with something deeper than policy.

There is a moral case for rural primacy, and it is this: the health of a civilization is measured not by the height of its towers but by the depth of its roots.

Cities are magnificent. I do not deny that. They produce art, innovation, commerce, and dynamism. But they also produce alienation, anonymity, dependency, and fragility.

Rural communities produce something cities cannot manufacture: rootedness. The knowledge that you belong to a place. That the land you work is the land your grandparents worked. That the neighbors who help you in crisis are the neighbors whose children grew up with yours. That your identity is not a brand to be curated but a life to be lived in full view of people who know your name.

That rootedness is not a luxury. It is the foundation of civic life. It is what makes self-governance possible. It is what makes sacrifice meaningful. It is what makes community real rather than theoretical.

And it is under threat—not because of inevitable economic forces, but because of choices. Policy choices. Investment choices. Cultural choices. Choices made overwhelmingly by people who live in cities, for the benefit of cities, with little regard for the communities that sustain them.

We can make different choices.

We can choose to prioritize the places where food is grown and energy is produced and children are raised in communities where everyone knows their name. We can choose to build a politics that reflects the geography of this vast nation rather than the density of a few zip codes. We can choose to build a culture that honors work, land, faith, and place rather than consumption, spectacle, and trend.

The Call

Rural America, hear me:

You are not a relic. You are not a problem to be solved. You are not a demographic to be managed. You are the backbone of the most extraordinary nation in human history, and it is long past time you stood up straight.

The cities did not ask permission to dominate. They accumulated power and wielded it. If we want the balance to shift, we must do the same—with discipline, with unity, with moral clarity, and with the unapologetic conviction that our way of life is not just worth preserving but worth advancing as the defining vision of American civilization.

This is not about tearing anything down. It is about building up what should have been built up all along.

The soil beneath your feet has waited long enough.

Let's get to work.

Thank you, and God bless Rural America—the true heart of these United States.
